title: Two Birds on One Tree
hookLine: two birds on one tree, one eating and one watching: Samkhya's purusha and prakriti
carry: purusha, the witness, is not the worry

cards: There's a picture so old it's in the Rig Veda, and the Upanishads keep it. Two birds, close friends, sit on the same tree.
One hops from branch to branch, eating the fruit, sweet and bitter, and every bite changes its mood. The other eats nothing. It just looks on.
The Mundaka Upanishad adds the turn: the eating bird, sunk in its troubles, grieves, until it looks up and sees the other one, the Lord, calm and content. Then its grief falls away.
Same tree, same branch, two very different birds.

teach.h: PRAKRITI: THE TREE, THE FRUIT, THE MOOD.
teach.b: Samkhya reads the picture in its own terms. The tree, the fruit, the hunger and every mood a bite brings belong to prakriti.
The Samkhya Karika calls prakriti the root, not made by anything; everything else unfolds out of it. Mountains, yes, and your body.
But here's the surprise: your senses, your mind, your thoughts, even your sense of being an I, sit on prakriti's side too. In Samkhya, a worry is as much part of nature as a cloud.
The watching one is purusha. The Karika describes it in a short string of words: a witness, a seer, neutral, standing apart, not the doer. Purusha doesn't think the thoughts; they show up before it.
The eating bird's grief, in Samkhya's reading, is a mix-up: the witness taking nature's moods as its own.
Here the schools part ways, and Hindus let them. The Upanishad, as you heard, calls the watching bird the Lord. Advaita Vedanta, still to come, reads the self as one.
The Karika counts many witnesses, one for each of us, and leaves God out of its count.

teach.h: YOU ARE NOT ONLY THE BIRD THAT EATS.
teach.b: But they share a teaching Hindus come back to again and again: you are not only the bird that eats. Many teachers call resting there sakshi bhava, being the witness.
Today, the dread before a test is real fruit on the tree. It isn't the one watching.

how: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and its map of purusha and prakriti is taught alongside the Yoga Sutras, which build on it. The two-birds verse is often taught in Hindu study groups, and resting as the witness, sakshi bhava, is a practice many teachers give.

o: a count of the days in the sacred calendar
a school that starts its count with seer and seen
a ritual for honoring the household's elders

games.q: the first two — tap the pairs.
p: the root, not made by anything

s: in Samkhya, the mind belongs to purusha
the mind, the senses and even the sense of I unfold from prakriti. purusha only sees.
the two-birds picture goes back to the Rig Veda
the Rig Veda has it, and the Mundaka and Shvetashvatara Upanishads keep it.
the Samkhya Karika teaches one purusha shared by everyone
the Karika argues for many: people are born, die and sense separately.

games.q: you're studying with a Samkhya teacher. she asks: your worry about tomorrow, which side of the line does it sit on?
games.why: in Samkhya, thoughts and worries are part of prakriti, fruit on the tree. purusha is the one they appear to.

practice: For a couple of minutes, let things show up: a sound from the street, an itch, a thought about tomorrow. Each time, don't push it away and don't follow it; just note, quietly, seen, as if from the branch above.
That's sakshi bhava, resting as the witness. If you pray, you can let a prayer be one more thing that rises and is seen. If you don't, the noting is the whole practice.

wordCard.voice: Samkhya. The school that starts its count with two: prakriti, the tree, the fruit and every mood, and purusha, the one who watches.

orig.note: Sanskrit: in Samkhya, the witness, the seer that stands apart from everything seen.

carryVoice: Your line: purusha, the witness, is not the worry. Two birds, one tree. Rest well.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.164.20 (two birds, companions, on one tree)
Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1–2 (one bird eats, one looks on; the grieving one sees the other and is freed from sorrow); also Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6–7
Samkhya Karika 3 (the root, prakriti, is not a product)
Samkhya Karika 19–20 (purusha as witness, neutral, seer, not an agent; through their union, purusha seems to act)
